<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Tuning a laser–wakefield accelerator to a desired electron energy spectrum is normally done by scanning the machine one setting at a time, which consumes scarce beam time and expert attention. We address the inverse problem directly, recovering the experimental settings that produce a target spectrum. To do so we train a conditional diffusion model, built on the Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Models (EDM) framework, on measured electron spectra from the ALFA beamline, conditioned on laser energy, gas-jet backing pressure, and gas-valve opening time. Because EDM samples by integrating a probability-flow ordinary differential equation, the map from settings to spectrum is differentiable end to end, and the settings themselves can be treated as free variables and optimized by backpropagation through the sampler. We propose and evaluate a three-stage strategy, BO
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mo accent="false" stretchy="false">→</mml:mo>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    L-BFGS
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mo accent="false" stretchy="false">→</mml:mo>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    RAdam, in which Bayesian optimization provides a global warm start across flat regions, L-BFGS exploits local curvature, and a final stochastic phase relaxes the solution away from sharp, bin-aligned minima. Against seven alternative single- and multi-stage strategies, this ordering recovers the target settings with the lowest mean squared error. We position this as a tool for differentiable inverse design in experiment planning, complementary to particle-in-cell simulation rather than a substitute for it.
                  </jats:p>
title: Differentiable control of laser–plasma experiments with conditional diffusion models

metadata.title: High-Repetition-Rate Laser-Driven Fast Neutron Generation from Planar Liquid Heavy Water Jets
metadata.summary: We demonstrate a high-repetition-rate, directional pitcher-catcher neutron source employing a continuously flowing, ambient-temperature liquid jet pitcher and a beryllium catcher target. Proton or deuteron beams are accelerated at 0.5 Hz from water (H$_{2}$O) or heavy water (D$_{2}$O) sheet jets using the $2ω$ ALEPH laser at Colorado State University. Deuteron-induced neutron generation shows an average flux enhancement in the target normal direction of 13x compared to proton-induced neutron generation, achieving peak fluxes of $7.9\times10^{5}$ neutrons/sr. The experimentally predicted ion-to-neutron conversion efficiency of 1.5$\times 10^{-5}$ for protons and 1.1$\times 10^{-3}$ for deuterons indicates a significant yield contribution from the deuteron breakup reaction. High shot-to-shot stability neutron spectra up to 8.7~MeV ($^9$Be(d,n)$^{10}$B) are observed for more than 200 consecutive shots.

metadata.title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
metadata.summary: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. We prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any number of particles (representation equivalence) and derive an error analysis that separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors: up to the learning error, NEOPIC has the error structure of standard Monte Carlo particle methods. We show that the particle noise in the training data acts as an implicit regularizer, which gives guidance on the number of training particles in relation to the particle numbers used at inference. A complexity analysis shows that NEOPIC is an $O(N_p)$ method whose constants are set by the architecture alone, independently of any mesh or tree. Numerical experiments on electrostatic benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap, confirm the theoretical findings. A single model trained on several mini-apps generated by different reference methods captures all of them and remains stable up to twice the training time window, which points towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.
